To wriggle means to make short, quick, twisting movements with your body — the kind of movements a worm makes as it moves across the ground. Picture a fish just caught in someone's hands, twisting and turning rapidly trying to get free. That is wriggling. The movements are small, repeated, and involve turning or bending, not just shaking.

This is the heart of the word. Keep that worm-like, twisting motion in your mind as you read everything below.

1. A person or animal wriggles when their whole body twists and turns.

The puppy wriggled with excitement when she picked it up.
The baby wriggled and refused to lie still while being dressed.
The earthworm wriggled slowly across the wet pavement.

Here, the subject is doing the wriggling — twisting their body repeatedly.

2. You can wriggle a specific body part, meaning you move it with small, twisting motions.

He wriggled his toes inside his boots to keep them warm.
She wriggled her fingers to check if anything was broken.

3. You can wriggle your way through, into, or out of a tight or difficult physical space. This is a very common and important use. When a space is too small or something is in your way, you twist and turn your body to get through it.

The cat wriggled through the narrow gap under the gate.
The child wriggled out from under the heavy blanket.
He wriggled into the tight wetsuit with great difficulty.
The thief wriggled through the small window.

The key idea here: wriggling is how you move when a direct, straight path is blocked. You can't just walk through — you have to twist, turn, and manoeuvre your body through the resistance.

4. A person wriggles when they are uncomfortable, restless, or nervous — they shift and twist in their seat or position, unable to stay still.

The student wriggled uncomfortably in her chair during the long lecture.
He wriggled with impatience while waiting in the long queue.

This is a very important non-physical use of the word, and you will encounter it constantly.

To wriggle out of something means to escape a duty, obligation, or difficult situation — not physically, but through clever excuses, clever talk, or by finding a loophole. Just as a worm wriggles free from a hand, a person "wriggles out of" a responsibility by twisting and turning around it.

He always wriggles out of washing the dishes.
She tried to wriggle out of the contract by finding a small clause.
Don't let him wriggle out of his responsibilities this time.
The politician wriggled out of answering the difficult question.

The feeling this phrase carries is mild disapproval or frustration — the person is being slippery and evasive. They are not confronting the situation directly; they are twisting around it.
The Full Range of Situations Where "Wriggle" Fits

To summarise the types of situations where you use this word:

  • An animal twisting and turning (a worm, a fish, a puppy)
  • A person twisting restlessly in their seat
  • A person squeezing their body through a tight space by twisting and turning
  • A person moving a body part with small, twisting motions (toes, fingers)
  • A person escaping an obligation through evasion (figurative)

Knowing similar words will sharpen your understanding of exactly what "wriggle" means.

Wiggle — lighter, smaller, and more playful movements. You wiggle your hips, wiggle a loose tooth. Wiggling doesn't really involve the whole body, and there is no sense of escaping something. It's more casual and cheerful.

She wiggled her hips to the music. (playful, rhythmic)
She wriggled out from under the fence. (purposeful, escaping)

Squirm — squirming is more about being trapped in discomfort or embarrassment and twisting because of that feeling. The emphasis is on the feeling (unease, shame, physical pain) rather than the motion. You squirm when you are stuck somewhere uncomfortable; you wriggle when you are trying to get through or get free.

He squirmed in embarrassment when she read his diary aloud. (stuck in shame)
He wriggled free from the rope. (active attempt to escape)

Writhe — much more intense and dramatic than wriggle. Writhing is associated with severe pain or extreme emotion — it is large, uncontrolled, and agonising.

She writhed in agony on the floor. (extreme pain)
The puppy wriggled in her arms. (small, lively movements)

The key distinction of "wriggle": It almost always has a sense of purposeful twisting against resistance — either getting through a tight space, getting free from a grip, or (figuratively) escaping a responsibility. The movements are small and repeated, and there is something being navigated or escaped.
A Few Final Examples to Cement the Word

The small child wriggled off her mother's lap and ran towards the toys.
The suspect wriggled free from the officer's grip and ran.
She wriggled her way to the front of the crowded room.
He's brilliant at wriggling out of trouble — he always has an excuse ready.
The kitten wriggled underneath the sofa and refused to come out.

To wriggle is to make small, repeated, twisting movements of the body — to move through tight spaces, to get free from something, or to shift restlessly; and figuratively, to cleverly escape a duty or commitment by being evasive.
